nodes.question: When was DEET first documented in fresh-water environments?
nodes.answer: DEET was first documented in fresh-water environments throughout the 1990s in American and European regions.
nodes.paragraph: The consump - tion of DEET at large doses has also been observed to exhibit fatal toxicity. A recent study reported that there is a significant correlation between DEET and increased levels of serum uric acid in the human population and the occurrence of several chronic ailments, including gout, diabetes, hypertension, and chronic renal illnesses [9]. Conventional municipal treatment plants are not designed to handle this type of pollutant. Due to its low log Kd (dissociation constant) value of 1.91, only a mini - mum proportion of DEET can be adsorbed into waste - water sludge, soils, and landfills [10]. This results in the migration of DEET into the aquatic environment, and the detected concentration range varies from ng/L to mg/L. The early documentation of DEET detection in fresh - water environments occurred throughout the 1990s in American and European regions. Due to the significant use of DEET in personal care products (PCPs) and their application in agriculture, the presence of DEET in waste - water, surface water, and groundwater has been observed [3, 11].

nodes.question: What methods are mentioned for obtaining genomic datasets?
nodes.answer: Double digest Restriction Associated DNA sequencing (RAD-seq) and sequence-capture methods are mentioned for obtaining genomic datasets.
nodes.paragraph: 2016; Camacho-S inchez et al. 2020; Sunde et al. 2020; Zimmerman et al. 2020; Dufresnes et al. 2023a). Genomic datasets obtained from double digest Restriction Associ- ated DNA sequencing (RAD-seq; Peterson et al. 2012) or sequence-capture methods (Hutter et al. 2022; de Visser et al. 2024) offer far greater resolving power to distinguish 363 Conservation Genetics (2025) 26:361 379 lineages and the structure therein, to accurately delineate their geographic boundaries, to quantify the extent of admix- ture, and to estimate population genetic diversity with fewer samples (Lexer et al. 2013; Vences et al. 2024). Although significantly improving the accuracy of infer - ences, the shift from genetic to genomic methods poses chal- lenges (Shaffer et al. 2015; Vences et al. 2024). Amphibian species are relatively weak dispersers among vertebrates (maximum a few kilometers per generation) and only occupy specific, sometimes disconnected habitats (Cayuela et al. 2020). Amphibian populations are thus expected to be locally structured, and analyses of thousands of loci may eventually recover every surveyed population as a distinct genetic cluster.

nodes.answer: Quantitative PCR (qPCR) using the QuantStudio 3 (Applied Biosystems, USA) was used to process the DNA samples after extraction.
nodes.paragraph: Calculating expulsion rates For each cell pellet resuspended and preserved in Lugols, four rounds of hemocytometer counts were conducted using an inverted microscope. Symbiodiniaceae expulsion rates were calculated by averaging the counts and using the following formula: A loss factor was incorporated into calculations to account for potential cell loss during the centrifugation process. An aliquot of axenic cultured symbionts was counted using the hemocytometer at culture density, diluted to 150 mL, then run through the centrifugation process and counted again. About 33% of cells were calculated as lost in the supernatant across replicates. Expulsion was calculated in terms of cells expelled per hour and standardized to coral tissue surface area (cm2) as determined from the photographs (ImageJ). nodes.question: What pathogen is associated with Desmodus rotundus in the context of this study?
nodes.answer: Desmodus rotundus is a reservoir for the rabies virus.
nodes.paragraph: Future climate change and the distributional shift of the common vampire bat, Desmodus rotundus Paige Van de Vuurst1,2,3, Julia M. Gohlke4,5 & Luis E. Escobar2,3,5 Interactions among humans, livestock, and wildlife within disturbed ecosystems, such as those impacted by climate change, can facilitate pathogen spillover transmission and increase disease emergence risks. The study of future climate change impacts on the distribution of free-ranging bats is therefore relevant for forecasting potential disease burden. This study used current and future climate data and historic occurrence locations of the vampire bat species Desmodus rotundus , a reservoir of the rabies virus to assess the potential impacts of climate change on disease reservoir distribution. Analyses included a comprehensive comparison of different climate change periods, carbon emission scenarios, and global circulation models (GCMs) on final model outputs. Models revealed that, although climatic scenarios and GCMs used have a significant influence on model outputs, there was a consistent signal of range expansion across the future climates analyzed. Areas suitable for D. rotundus range expansion include the southern United States and south-central portions of Argentina and Chile. Certain areas in the Amazon Rainforest, which currently rests at the geographic center of D. rotundus range, may become climatically unsuitable for this species within the context of niche conservatism.
